## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mudupāṇijātaka* (Ja 262) is a birth story preserved in the Pali Jātaka collection. Its verse opens with the incipit *Pāṇi ce muduko cassa* [Fausböll 1879]. In the introductory narrative, the Buddha delivers the discourse while residing at Jetavana on account of a discontented monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*) [Fausböll 1879]. The Master observes that it is impossible to keep women from pursuing their desires, remarking that even ancient wise men could not guard their daughters, who managed to transgress with paramours even while holding their fathers' hands [Fausböll 1879]. At the conclusion of the story, the discontented monk attains the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), and the Buddha completes the birth identification (*samodhāna*), stating that he himself was the king at that time [Fausböll 1879].

DharmaNexus records no cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan literature [DharmaNexus].
